analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% surtax on individual income above $2 million ($1 million for single filers).
analysis.headline: The Millionaires Surtax Act never got a hearing, a vote, or a House companion; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 10% surtax on top of existing income taxes for the highest-earning individuals: single filers making over $1 million and couples making over $2 million in a year. It applies to modified adjusted gross income, so it reaches income from wages, investments, and business profits alike. The bill contains only the tax; it does not specify what the revenue would fund. Introduced by Senator Van Hollen in June 2021, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and no action ever followed.
analysis.who_benefits: The direct beneficiaries are the roughly 0.5% of households with incomes above the thresholds, but only through a burden shifted the other way: the bill does not cut anyone's taxes, so its benefit to ordinary people is indirect — it is a step toward asking the highest earners to shoulder more of federal costs, and its revenue would be available for whatever future Congresses choose to fund.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a new 10% surtax on each dollar of modified adjusted gross income above $2 million for joint filers and $1 million for single filers, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 [S3].

Because the tax applies to modified adjusted gross income, it reaches high earners regardless of whether their income comes from salary, investments, or business profits, rather than applying only to wages [S3].
The bill includes special rules to cover nonresident aliens and U.S. citizens living abroad, closing easy ways for high earners to escape the tax by moving income or residence offshore [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals whose income exceeds $1 million ($2 million for joint filers) would pay an additional 10% of their income above those thresholds. This is a small group of the highest-earning households. Nonprofit charitable trusts are exempted. The bill does not say what the revenue would be used for, so no one gains a specific benefit unless a future law directs it.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue without directing it anywhere; a surtax on its own does not fund any program, cut any deficit, or lower any other tax, so its practical value depends entirely on what future legislation does with the money [S2].

The thresholds are high and indexed to nothing in the bill, so inflation over time would not widen the surtax but the tax would not address taxpayers earning between, say, $400,000 and $1 million, whom many tax proposals also target [S3].

A good-faith objection is that a 10% surtax on top of existing rates could push top federal rates on marginal income to the highest levels in decades, and critics of high-income tax increases argue this discourages investment and encourages income shifting; the bill does partially accommodate this by excluding the investment interest deduction from the base [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward, narrow ask: the highest-earning sliver of households pays an extra 10% on income above $1-2 million, and everyone else pays nothing. The design is simple and hard to game — it applies to total modified adjusted gross income and has anti-avoidance rules for people abroad. Its main weakness is that it is revenue with no destination: as a standalone bill it accomplishes nothing unless paired with a spending or tax bill that uses the money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the session ended with it still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act on June 10, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Three Senate Democrats — Brown, Klobuchar, and Merkley — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee's only action on the bill was the initial referral; no further committee or floor action appears in the bill's history through the end of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill was a standalone measure; major tax legislation in this Congress moved through different vehicles, and this surtax was not incorporated into any of them [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $1 million (or $2 million for joint filers) are better off because the bill never advanced — they owe no 10% surtax on income above those thresholds. Everyone else's tax situation is unchanged, and the revenue that could have been raised from top earners was never collected.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; none of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where party lines could be counted.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill would take an additional 10% of every dollar of their income above $1-2 million. Their interest in blocking it runs against any use of that revenue for broader public purposes.

industries.industry: Wealth management and tax advisory firms serving ultra-high-net-worth clients
industries.note: A new surtax on top earners would increase demand for income-shifting and planning services, but wealthy clients would pay advisors to minimize it. The industry's stake is in the outcome, not the public's.
